title: Financial Statement Intelligence Engine
description: Type a company name, get its financial health, in any market: US, Europe, India, Japan. US listings use 10 years of SEC EDGAR filings; everywhere else uses Yahoo Finance. Also runs as a 20-company batch producing a 23-page report.
highlights: Works for any listed company, not a fixed list. A Streamlit app takes a name or ticker, resolves it (including cross-listings, which it shows rather than silently picking one), and scores it live. Verified across five markets: Apple through EDGAR at 10 years, ASML, Shell, Nestle and Reliance through Yahoo Finance.

Currency is where a global loader silently produces a plausible wrong answer instead of an error, and three traps are handled: London quotes in pence, not pounds (Shell's "3320.0" GBp read as GBP overstates the price 100x); the reporting currency is not always the quote currency (Infosys reports in USD, trades in INR); and the currency flag itself lies in both directions (HCL Technologies is tagged USD while reporting in rupees). The check is market capitalisation, which is unambiguously in the quote currency — except between currencies of similar size (USD vs GBP at 0.79), where that test can't discriminate and the source's own tag is used instead.
Foreign issuers file 20-F, not 10-K, so EDGAR returns nothing for Shell or SAP despite both being US-listed. The loader falls back to Yahoo Finance automatically rather than failing.

Every figure comes from filed 10-K data via the SEC EDGAR XBRL API for US companies, across 20 companies and 10 fiscal years in the batch report. Nothing is hand-entered, and the spot checks tie out to the filings (NVIDIA FY2025 revenue $130.5B, Microsoft FY2025 $281.7B, Tesla 2024 $97.69B).

Most of the engineering went into making EDGAR usable. Companies migrate between GAAP tags mid-history after ASC 606, so values are merged across an ordered list of candidate tags rather than taken from the first tag that returns anything, which took NVIDIA and Tesla from 6 usable years to 10.

Oil majors and several pharma companies never tag an operating income line, so EBIT is rebuilt from pretax income plus interest expense. Without that fallback, Exxon, Chevron, J&J, Merck and Pfizer produced no usable years at all.

EPS growth is deliberately excluded from the score. A 10-K restates only the roughly three years it covers, so Apple's FY2018 EPS reads 11.91 in one filing and 2.98 in another after the 4-for-1 split. Growth is scored on revenue and net income, which splits cannot distort.

The score refuses to invent results where data is missing: unavailable metrics are dropped, the remaining weights in that pillar are renormalized, and the exclusions are disclosed on each company's page. This caught negative book equity at Home Depot and AbbVie, where a negative debt-to-equity had been clamping to a perfect leverage score and overstating AbbVie by four points.

The resulting ranking is the clearest evidence of the method's own weakness, which is the point. The top four are all asset-light software and advertising businesses while Walmart lands 18th, because absolute thresholds measure the business model more than how well the company is run. Peer-relative scoring is the next module.

Full threshold table, fiscal-year convention and known limitations are published in the report and README, so any score can be recalculated or argued with. Backed by 26 tests covering the negative-equity, zero-interest, weight-renormalization and currency-resolution edge cases.

title: Institutional-Style Valuation Engine
description: Valuation engine for Nifty (NSE) companies in INR. Stages 1 to 6 are built end to end: historical assumptions, forecast, FCFF, WACC, a discounted cash flow, comparable-company valuation, and bull/base/bear scenarios with sensitivity tables. The DCF and comparables currently disagree, the entry explains why with evidence rather than picking one, and neither is published as a quoted number until that is resolved. Monte Carlo is next.
highlights: The DCF reads every one of 32 companies below market price. Rather than publish that or quietly tune an assumption until it agreed, Stage 5 built a second, independent valuation method (comparable-company multiples) specifically to test whether the gap was a bug or a real limitation, and it settled the question: median comparables upside is +2.9%, close to fair value, against the DCF's -72.6%, built from the identical underlying statements and market data. A shared-input bug would have dragged both methods off in the same direction; it didn't, which points at the DCF's terminal-value mechanism specifically.

The pattern confirms it. TCS: -9.8% on comparables against -27.8% on the DCF. Hindustan Unilever, fully domestic and asset-light, shows the single largest DCF gap in the universe at 7.5 points of implied discount rate, near risk-free. The gap is largest for exactly the highest-quality, lowest-growth, most richly-rated compounders, which is the textbook failure mode of a Gordon-growth terminal value fed a conservative, GDP-capped growth rate: the market pays for stability and optionality beyond the forecast horizon that a perpetuity formula does not capture.

A genuine correctness bug was found and fixed along the way, and is kept distinct from the finding above rather than conflated with it. Terminal-year reinvestment was made consistent with terminal growth, but the five explicit forecast years still held capex at its historical share of revenue while growth faded down underneath them. Capex now fades toward its terminal-consistent level across the whole forecast, the same way revenue growth already fades toward terminal growth. It moved Reliance from an unusable 22 rupees a share to 323, but testing afterward showed it barely moved the universe-wide gap, which is what pointed at Stage 5 as the next real diagnostic rather than more capex tuning.

The equity risk premium was deliberately not lowered to close the gap. It was checked first: building the cost of equity through dollars instead (US risk-free plus a mature ERP plus a country premium, adjusted for the inflation differential) lands at the same 14.5%, so 7.5% is defensible on its own terms. Lowering it anyway would have treated the symptom rather than the cause.

Comparable-company valuation values a company off what the market pays for its sector peers rather than off its own cash-flow forecast. Peer selection is sector membership fixed independently of any single run, so it cannot be adjusted per company toward a wanted answer, and a company with fewer than two usable peers is reported as unusable rather than valued off a group too thin to mean anything: 8 of 32 companies fall into that category here. A multiple is excluded, not clamped, when its denominator is negative or near zero, and outliers are flagged by median absolute deviation rather than silently dropped.

Bull, base and bear (Stage 6) are each a full, independently recomputed valuation, not a percentage haircut on the base case: a real downside compounds compressed margins, slower growth, a higher discount rate and a duller terminal outlook together, which a flat -20% cannot represent. Testing an extreme case (a levered, structurally declining company) surfaced a real bug before it reached anyone: negative equity value was being printed as a literal negative share price, which no equity can trade at under limited liability. The model now keeps the honest raw number for anyone measuring how far underwater a business is, but headline output and computed upside floor at zero, capping downside at -100% rather than reporting past it.

WACC is built from its components rather than assumed: CAPM cost of equity with beta from a regression of monthly returns against the Nifty 50, Blume-adjusted for mean reversion; cost of debt as interest over average debt, bounded on both sides after Hindustan Unilever's naive calculation came back at 26%; and weights at market value of equity, book value of debt.

FCFF is built the unlevered way and tested for it. Tax is charged on EBIT and interest never enters the cash flow, because the reported tax charge is struck after interest and already carries the debt tax shield. Using it while WACC also carries the shield in the discount rate values the same benefit twice, which is the most common way a DCF flatters itself and always moves the answer up.

Working capital anchors on the recent level, not the ten-year median. Building it the obvious way would have produced a phantom multi-billion first-year cash outflow for Apple, whose working capital moved from +5% of revenue to -10% across the decade, so the median described no state the business was ever in.

Checking the output against reality caught a currency bug worth more than the rest of the module. yfinance returns Infosys statements in USD while the share quotes in INR, which would have divided its valuation by about 95. The obvious fix was also wrong: HCL Technologies carries the same USD flag while reporting in rupees, so trusting the flag overstated it a hundredfold. The currency is now inferred by testing which reading implies a believable price-to-sales ratio against market capitalisation.

74 tests across the six stages, covering the reinvestment identity, currency resolution in both directions, multiple exclusion on negative or near-zero denominators, scenario ordering and independence, sensitivity-grid monotonicity, and the negative-equity floor.

title: Live Institutional Risk Engine
description: A live risk-monitoring engine: any listed company or benchmark in, market risk recalculated on demand. Phases 1 to 3 of 14 are built: data ingestion with tiered validation, returns, historical and rolling volatility, and beta and drawdown, each verified against real, documented market events rather than only synthetic tests. VaR, Expected Shortfall, GARCH, stress testing and the live dashboard are the phases still to come.
highlights: Every fetch is timestamped and classified DELAYED or STALE by measured age, never LIVE, because yfinance carries no real-time service guarantee. "Live" in this engine means refreshable on demand and recalculated from current data, not real-time, and the code states that distinction rather than quietly claiming more than the data source supports.

Data validation is tiered rather than pass/fail: issues are corrected automatically (a duplicate date, an out-of-order row), warnings let the calculation proceed but flag what to read carefully (a data gap, an extreme single-day move), and blocking issues refuse the series outright with "Insufficient data for reliable risk calculation" rather than a confident wrong number. The cleaning function applies exactly the corrections the validator describes, so the two can never quietly disagree.

Verified against real, documented events rather than only synthetic fixtures. NVIDIA's June 2024 10:1 stock split produces no false extreme-move flag, and checking why revealed that yfinance's close price is already split-adjusted regardless of the auto_adjust flag, which corrected a wrong assumption in the code's own comments before it shipped. GameStop's May 2024 short-squeeze days are correctly flagged as extreme moves, confirming the detector responds to genuine events.

Beta is computed two independent ways from the same data (the covariance formula and OLS regression) and the two results are asserted equal at runtime, since they are mathematically the same estimator and any gap between them means an alignment bug, not a modelling choice. A confidence field travels with every beta: Coca-Cola showed a near-zero beta against the S&P 500 over the last three years, which was checked rather than assumed to be a bug (the alignment and statistics were sound), and is reported as a genuinely low-confidence reading rather than hidden.

Two modules built and tested completely independently, the volatility-spike detector and the drawdown-episode detector, found the same elevated-risk period in the S&P 500's 2025 history without being told to look for it, which is stronger evidence of correctness than either module passing its own tests alone. Drawdown also reconstructed the real 2022 bear market exactly: -25.4% from January to October 2022, recovering by January 2024.

50 tests, including a flaky one caught and fixed by diagnosing the actual cause (a 5% significance threshold producing an expected 1-in-20 false positive on independent data) rather than just swapping the random seed until it passed.

title: AI Financial Research Analyst (RAG)
description: A retrieval-augmented research agent that answers investment questions by calling the financial, valuation and risk engines as tools and citing the filing, page and section behind every claim.
highlights: The LLM never calculates or invents a financial figure; it calls dedicated financial-statement, valuation and risk tools and reports what they return.
RAG retrieves the actual annual-report or filing section behind an answer before the model responds, so "why did margins decline" is answered from a real disclosure, not a guess.
Every research response is labeled as source-derived fact, model-derived calculation, or AI interpretation, so a reader knows which parts to trust and which to check.
Confidence scoring and a data-freshness check let the system say "insufficient evidence" instead of producing a fluent but unsupported answer.
An audit log records what was retrieved and which tools fired for every answer, so a research conclusion can be traced back and reproduced.

title: Investment Committee Dashboard
description: A six-page decision terminal that turns financial analysis, valuation, risk and AI research into one BUY/HOLD/SELL memo, stating the explicit thresholds that would change the call.
highlights: Six pages, not one screen: overview, financial analysis, valuation, risk, AI research and an investment-committee memo, each built for a different reviewer's question.
The memo states the recommendation alongside the specific financial thresholds that would flip it, rather than a static, one-time conclusion.
Every chart on the valuation and risk pages links back to the same underlying model output the AI analyst cites, so the dashboard and the AI never disagree.
Designed to answer whether the company is healthy, what it's worth, and what could go wrong within a few minutes for someone seeing it for the first time.
